target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is a productive use of animals because over 98% are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills.
objection: Dissection specimens are not simply harmless byproducts: AG2 argues that about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, so the practice relies on a supply chain that harms animals and the environment by reducing local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection provides educational benefits worth keeping.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations are available and, according to AG2, teach biology equally well or better than dissecting dead animals, so students can meet the same learning goals without using real animals.

target: AG1’s implicit assumption that dissection is justified by necessity in biology or medical training.
objection: AG2 argues there is no curricular or medical-training necessity for animal dissection because it is not required by AP Biology or Next Generation Science Standards and U.S./Canadian medical schools do not use animals to train physicians.

target: AG2’s claim that typical dissection depends on wild-catching and biodiversity loss despite AG1’s byproduct/already-dead framing.
objection: AG1 objects that, in typical classroom use, over 98% of dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, so classroom dissection does not materially depend on wild-catching animals or meaningfully cause biodiversity loss.

target: AG1’s rebuttal that most specimens are already dead/byproducts and therefore dissection does not materially depend on wild-caught animals.
objection: AG2 responds that even if many specimens are byproducts or already dead, the existence of a wild-caught component means dissection demand still sustains wild capture for part of the supply, so the biodiversity harm is not eliminated.

target: AG2’s claim that non-animal alternatives can teach equally well or better, including the fine-motor and hand-eye-coordination benefits of dissection.
objection: AG1 argues that those physical skills depend on real manipulation of tissues and tools, and synthetic models or computer simulations do not provide the same hands-on experience with real tissues, so they cannot be assumed to teach equally well.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection uniquely builds fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and motivation.
objection: AG2 replies that such skills mainly come from tool handling, repeated practice, and spatial reasoning, which synthetic or manipulable non-animal models can also provide; likewise, interactive non-animal activities can still create engagement and “aha moments,” so these benefits are not unique to real animals.

target: AG1’s assumption that authentic anatomical variability makes real dissection necessary for critical-thinking development.
objection: AG2 contends that synthetic models and simulations can also support critical-thinking learning goals, so real-animal dissection is not necessary even for higher-level reasoning outcomes.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s byproduct/already-dead nature makes it acceptable despite harms.
objection: AG2 argues that dissection still entails serious animal and environmental harms through wild-capture supply chains, so the practice remains harmful even if some specimens are already dead or byproducts.

target: AG1’s attempt to justify dissection mainly on educational value while downplaying other harms.
objection: AG2 adds that school dissection creates avoidable environmental and health harms through hazardous chemical fixatives and biohazard waste, over and above any harm from the animals themselves.

AG1 responds that in school labs these chemicals and wastes are handled through established safety procedures and regulated disposal, so the harms are manageable rather than an inherently large or decisive reason to ban dissection.

target: AG2’s focus on dissection waste as a decisive harm compared with alternatives.
objection: AG1 argues that fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts that would otherwise be landfilled, so dissection can divert them from landfill and reduce environmental harm rather than merely creating waste.

target: AG2’s implication that non-animal alternatives avoid the relevant environmental/health harms altogether.
objection: AG1 counters that non-animal classroom methods still involve lab processes such as material handling, cleaning, sterilization, sharps handling, and waste disposal, so switching away from dissection does not reliably eliminate environmental or health harms; it mainly changes their form.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection should be banned because non-animal alternatives can replace it without losing educational value.
objection: AG1 says non-animal methods cannot be assumed to match the fine-motor, hand-eye-coordination, and authentic critical-thinking benefits of physically dissecting real specimens, so they are not clearly an equivalent substitute.

target: AG2’s argument that dissection’s harms make it avoidable because alternatives can deliver the same learning outcomes.
objection: AG1 insists the ban presupposes that non-animal options can provide the core learning benefits without sacrificing the instructional value of real dissection, which AG1 disputes.

target: AG1’s claim that because dissection provides benefits and uses mostly byproducts, it should be allowed.
objection: AG2 reasserts that dissection still typically causes serious environmental harm through the wild-capture supply chain, so the practice is harmful even if specimens are often byproducts.

target: AG1’s justification for dissection based on educational necessity.
objection: AG2 also argues that dissection is not required for core biology standards and that synthetic models/computer simulations can teach anatomy and structure instead, so the educational goals can be met without animal dissection.
